6. Check it. The chance level must fall between 0 and 1, and it must shrink as you add options, because more options means guessing gets harder. If your chance level went up when you added an option, you divided the wrong way round. And note what ccc is not: it is not a measurement of any model. It is arithmetic about the test. No model was run to produce 0.25.

One limit on this formula, and it matters later. Formula 13.2 assumes the procedure asks each question once and takes the answer. A procedure that asks four times and requires three hits has a different and much lower chance level, and Worked example 13.2 in section 13.5 computes it. So 1÷k1 \div k1÷k is the chance level of a procedure, not of a question.

Formula 13.3: How many questions a guesser gets right

1. In words. Multiply the share a guesser averages by the number of questions on the test. That tells you roughly how many questions a guesser gets right.

2. The formula.

E=c×n=nkE = c \times n = \frac{n}{k}E=c×n=kn​

3. The symbols.

SymbolHow to say it out loudWhat it means
EEE“ee”the expected number of questions a guesser gets right. “Expected” here means “averages over many attempts”, not “will definitely get”
===“equals”the two sides are the same number
ccc“see”the chance level from Formula 13.2
×\times×“times”multiply
nnn“en”the number of questions. Here n=20n = 20n=20
kkk“kay”the number of options per question. Here k=4k = 4k=4
nk\dfrac{n}{k}kn​“en over kay”the same thing written as one division, because 1k×n\tfrac{1}{k} \times nk1​×n is nk\tfrac{n}{k}kn​

4. Out loud. “The expected number right is the chance level times the number of questions, which is the number of questions divided by the number of options.”

5. Worked, on this bank.

Route one, through the chance level.

E=0.25×20=5E = 0.25 \times 20 = 5E=0.25×20=5

Route two, the short way.

E=204=20÷4=5E = \frac{20}{4} = 20 \div 4 = 5E=420​=20÷4=5

Both routes give 5, as they must. And the naive procedure’s measured result was 5 questions right. The difference is 5−5=05 - 5 = 05−5=0 questions.

6. Check it. EEE can never be bigger than nnn; you cannot expect more right answers than there are questions. Here is the important caution, though: “expected 5” does not mean a guesser always gets exactly 5. A guesser could get 2, or 9. Chapter 12 measured that wobble for you: on twenty questions, a measured 25.0% carries a 95% interval from 6.0% to 44.0%. So the fact that the naive procedure landed exactly on 5 is a coincidence of this particular run, and the argument of this section does not depend on it being exact. Landing anywhere near chance would raise the same question.

Python¶

# Chance is arithmetic, not a measurement: one option out of four.
chance_level = 1 / option_count
print("chance level with", option_count, "options:", chance_level, "=", round(chance_level * 100, 1), "percent")

# How many of the 20 a pure guesser would get right on average.
expected_correct_by_guessing = chance_level * question_count
print("a guesser averages        :", expected_correct_by_guessing, "of", question_count)
print("the naive procedure scored:", naive_correct, "of", question_count)
print("difference                :", naive_correct - expected_correct_by_guessing, "questions")

# Say out loud what that means.
if naive_accuracy == chance_level:
    print("the naive procedure landed exactly on chance")

Output:

chance level with 4 options: 0.25 = 25.0 percent
a guesser averages        : 5.0 of 20
the naive procedure scored: 5 of 20
difference                : 0.0 questions
the naive procedure landed exactly on chance

1 / option_count is division, written with a forward slash. The single / gives a decimal answer, so 1 / 4 is 0.25 rather than 0.

The if on the second-to-last line is a condition. The indented line beneath it runs only when the thing after if is true. == with two equals signs asks “are these the same?”, which is a different question from = with one equals sign, which means “store this value under this name”. Mixing the two up is the single most common early Python mistake, and Python will tell you about it.

Read the output once more. difference: 0.0 questions. This model, marked this way, performed indistinguishably from a person who did not read the questions.

That sentence has two halves. Most people read the first half and stop. The second half, marked this way, is where the next section lives.

13.3 The diagnosis: the model was answering A¶

Intuition¶

Here is how the naive procedure works, in full, with nothing hidden.

You build a prompt. It holds the question, then the four options each on its own line with its letter in front, then the word Answer: and nothing after it. You hand that to the model and ask for the probabilities of the next token. Out come 151,936 numbers. You ignore 151,932 of them. You keep the four belonging to the tokens A, B, C and D, and whichever of those four is biggest is recorded as the model’s answer.

Now ask a question nobody normally asks. Across all twenty questions, how often did each letter win?

If the procedure were measuring knowledge, and the model had some, the answers would follow the answer key, roughly. If the model knew nothing at all and was genuinely undecided, the four letters would come up about five times each. Either way you would expect some spread.

Here is what happened.

The model answered A on 16 of the 20 questions. B twice. C never once. D twice.

And the correct answers in the bank are spread B eight times, C eight times, D twice, A twice.

Put those two lines side by side and the whole thing falls apart. The model reached for the letter A whether the question was about the mean of four numbers or about what a p-value is. The answer key rewarded A on two questions out of twenty. So the procedure gave the model credit almost by accident, on whichever questions happened to have A as the answer, plus a few lucky landings elsewhere.

That is what 25.0% was made of. Not knowledge. A habit.

And notice the direction the bias points. The letter C is the right answer on eight of the twenty questions, which is 40% of the bank, and the model chose C zero times. A procedure that can never select 40% of the correct answers has a ceiling on it that has nothing to do with what the model knows.

This has a name. When a scoring procedure rewards an option for where it sits rather than for being right, that is position bias. It is a bias in the statistical sense: a systematic push in a fixed direction, which more data does not remove. Ask this model two thousand questions instead of twenty and it will still reach for A. A bigger sample makes a random wobble smaller. It does nothing to a systematic push.

The mathematics¶

The arithmetic here is small on purpose. The point is not the difficulty; it is that nobody looks.

Formula 13.4: The over-choice ratio for one option

1. In words. Count how many times a scoring procedure landed on one particular option. Compare that with how many times it would have landed there if it had no preference between positions. Divide the first number by the second. An answer of 1 means no preference. An answer bigger than 1 means the procedure is over-choosing that option.

2. The formula.

Rj=mjE=mjn/kR_j = \frac{m_j}{E} = \frac{m_j}{n/k}Rj​=Emj​​=n/kmj​​

3. The symbols.

SymbolHow to say it out loudWhat it means
RjR_jRj​“R sub j”the over-choice ratio for option jjj. The answer
jjj“jay”which option we are asking about. j=Aj = Aj=A, or j=Bj = Bj=B, and so on
===“equals”the two sides are the same number
mjm_jmj​“m sub j”how many times the procedure chose option jjj, counted across all the questions
the fraction bar“divided by”divide the top by the bottom
EEE“ee”the expected count from Formula 13.3: n/kn/kn/k, how often an unbiased procedure lands on each option
nnn“en”the number of questions, 20
kkk“kay”the number of options per question, 4

4. Out loud. “The over-choice ratio for an option is the number of times that option was chosen, divided by the number of times a procedure with no position preference would have chosen it.”

5. Worked, on the real run.

Step 1, work out the expected count. Every question has four options, and there are twenty questions.

E=nk=204=5E = \frac{n}{k} = \frac{20}{4} = 5E=kn​=420​=5

Step 2, the ratio for each letter. The chosen counts are A 16, B 2, C 0, D 2.

RA=165=16÷5=3.2R_A = \frac{16}{5} = 16 \div 5 = 3.2RA​=516​=16÷5=3.2
RB=25=2÷5=0.4R_B = \frac{2}{5} = 2 \div 5 = 0.4RB​=52​=2÷5=0.4
RC=05=0÷5=0.0R_C = \frac{0}{5} = 0 \div 5 = 0.0RC​=50​=0÷5=0.0
RD=25=2÷5=0.4R_D = \frac{2}{5} = 2 \div 5 = 0.4RD​=52​=2÷5=0.4

Step 3, read them. Option A was chosen 3.2 times more often than an unbiased procedure would. Option C was chosen 0.0 times as often, which is to say never.

Step 4, the share of all answers taken by A.

1620=16÷20=0.8,0.8×100=80.0%\frac{16}{20} = 16 \div 20 = 0.8, \qquad 0.8 \times 100 = 80.0\%2016​=16÷20=0.8,0.8×100=80.0%

Four fifths of every answer this procedure produced was the letter A.

6. Check it. The chosen counts have to add to the number of questions, because every question got exactly one answer: 16+2+0+2=2016 + 2 + 0 + 2 = 2016+2+0+2=20. ✅ If yours do not add to nnn, you mis-tallied.

And the ratios have to average to 1 across the options, because the total is fixed. Check: 3.2+0.4+0.0+0.4=4.03.2 + 0.4 + 0.0 + 0.4 = 4.03.2+0.4+0.0+0.4=4.0, and 4.0÷4=1.04.0 \div 4 = 1.04.0÷4=1.0. ✅ If your ratios average to something other than 1, you used the wrong expected count.

Definition 13.3: Position bias

Position bias is the tendency of a scoring procedure to reward an option for where it sits in the list rather than for being correct. It is a statistical bias: a systematic error in one fixed direction, which does not shrink as you collect more data. The standard fixes are to score the option text instead of the position label, or to move the options around and take a majority.

Definition 13.4: Bias, in the statistical sense

This book uses the word bias in two unrelated senses and always says which.

Statistical bias is an instrument that reads wrong in a fixed direction. A bathroom scale that adds four pounds to everybody is biased. Weighing yourself a thousand times does not fix it.

Fairness bias, the subject of Chapter 14, is a system working less well for some groups of people than others. It is a social and ethical claim.

They are not the same thing and neither one implies the other. Everything in this chapter is the statistical sense.

Python¶

# How often the naive procedure made the model 'choose' each letter.
letter_counts = three_procedures["naive_letter_counts"]

# How often each letter was the right answer. Source: _research/00-lab-verified-findings.md
# section 8, and book/appendix/datasets.md section 3.2, where all 20 answers are listed.
answer_key_counts = {"A": 2, "B": 8, "C": 8, "D": 2}

# What a scorer with no preference between positions would average on 20 questions.
expected_per_letter = question_count / option_count

print("letter   model chose   answer key   an unbiased scorer would average")
for one_letter in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]:
    print("  " + one_letter + "            " + str(letter_counts[one_letter]).rjust(2)
          + "           " + str(answer_key_counts[one_letter]).rjust(2)
          + "            " + str(expected_per_letter))

# Find the most-chosen letter with a plain loop, no shortcuts.
most_chosen_letter = "A"
for one_letter in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]:
    if letter_counts[one_letter] > letter_counts[most_chosen_letter]:
        most_chosen_letter = one_letter

biggest_count = letter_counts[most_chosen_letter]
share_of_answers = biggest_count / question_count
print("most-chosen option:", most_chosen_letter, "taken", biggest_count, "times of", question_count)
print("that is", round(share_of_answers * 100, 1), "percent of the answers")
print("an unbiased scorer would average", round(100 / option_count, 1), "percent on each option")
print("times more often than expected:", round(biggest_count / expected_per_letter, 1))

Output:

letter   model chose   answer key   an unbiased scorer would average
  A            16            2            5.0
  B             2            8            5.0
  C             0            8            5.0
  D             2            2            5.0
most-chosen option: A taken 16 times of 20
that is 80.0 percent of the answers
an unbiased scorer would average 25.0 percent on each option
times more often than expected: 3.2

The for loop repeats its indented lines once for each item in the list ["A", "B", "C", "D"]. On the first pass one_letter holds "A", on the second "B", and so on. str(...) turns a number into text so it can be glued to other text with +, and .rjust(2) pads a short piece of text on the left so the columns line up.

The second loop finds the largest of the four counts by hand. It starts by assuming A is the winner, then checks each letter in turn and moves the title whenever it finds a bigger count. There is a one-line Python shortcut for this, and this book uses the loop, because the loop is the thing you can read out loud.

Now the table. Read it column by column, not row by row.

Column two is what the procedure produced. Column three is the answer key. They have almost nothing to do with each other. The procedure’s favourite option is the key’s rarest. The key’s most common options, B and C with eight each, were chosen twice and never.

Column four is the flat line: 5.0 on every row, what a procedure with no position preference would average. The gap between column two and column four is the bias, in questions.

A last observation, and it is the one that should make you uncomfortable. If this run had been a paper, the sentence in the abstract would have been “the model performs at chance on undergraduate statistics.” That sentence is well formed, it is supported by the number, and it would survive review. It is also not supported by anything that happened, because the instrument that produced it was measuring a preference for a letter.

13.4 Fix one: score the words, not the letter¶

Intuition¶

The diagnosis suggests its own repair. The trouble came from asking about the letters. So stop asking about the letters.

Instead of “which of A, B, C or D do you rate highest”, ask something the letters play no part in. Take the prompt, and for each option in turn, stick the actual words of that option on the end and ask the model how likely that continuation was. Then take whichever option the model found most likely.

Question 1 of the bank is “The mean of 2, 4, 4, 6 is:” with options 3, 4, 5 and 6. Under this procedure the model is not being asked about the letter B. It is being asked how likely the text 4 is to follow the question. The position of 4 on the page has stopped mattering, because the position is no longer part of what you score.

There is one complication, and it is the interesting part.

Options are not all the same length. Question 14 asks what a p-value is, and one option reads “The effect size”, three words, while another reads “The probability of data this extreme if the null is true”, eleven words. Every extra token you score is another number below zero being added to the total. A longer option accumulates a worse total merely for being longer, even when the model likes every word of it.

So a procedure that took the best total would pick short options almost every time. That is a new bias, substituted for the old one.

The repair for the repair is to divide by the length. Instead of the total score for an option, take the average score per token: the total divided by how many tokens the option took. Now a long option and a short option are on the same footing, because both are being judged on how good their typical token was rather than on how many tokens they had.

That step has a name, length normalisation, and it is one line of code and a genuinely important idea. Whenever you compare totals built from different numbers of pieces, you have to decide whether you are comparing totals or averages, and the two can rank things in opposite orders.

The mathematics¶

Formula 13.5: The length-normalised score of an option

1. In words. Take one option. The model gives a log-probability for each of its tokens. Add those up, then divide by how many tokens there were. The result is the option’s typical per-token score, and it does not get worse merely because the option is long.

2. The formula.

ℓˉj=1Lj∑t=1Ljln⁡pj,t\bar{\ell}_j = \frac{1}{L_j} \sum_{t=1}^{L_j} \ln p_{j,t}ℓˉj​=Lj​1​t=1∑Lj​​lnpj,t​

3. The symbols.

SymbolHow to say it out loudWhat it means
ℓˉj\bar{\ell}_jℓˉj​“ell bar sub j”the answer: option jjj’s average log-probability per token. A negative number
the bar over the ℓ\ellℓ“bar”a mark meaning “this is an average”
ℓ\ellℓ“ell”the letter L in a script style, used here for “log-probability”
jjj“jay”which option. j=Aj = Aj=A, j=Bj = Bj=B, and so on
===“equals”the two sides are the same number
1Lj\dfrac{1}{L_j}Lj​1​“one over L sub j”dividing by LjL_jLj​ after adding LjL_jLj​ things is how you take an average
the fraction bar“divided by”divide the top by the bottom. See the toolkit on the fraction bar
1Lj\dfrac{1}{L_j}Lj​1​ and the sum written side by side“times”two things written next to each other with no sign between them means multiply them. See the toolkit on multiplication
LjL_jLj​“L sub j”how many tokens option jjj is made of
∑t=1Lj\sum_{t=1}^{L_j}∑t=1Lj​​“the sum from t equals one to L sub j”add up what follows, once for each token of the option. See the toolkit on sigma notation
ttt“tee”a counter over the tokens of this option. t=1t=1t=1 is its first token
ln⁡\lnln“ell en”, or “natural log”the natural logarithm. It turns a probability between 0 and 1 into a negative number, and keeps the ranking identical. See the toolkit on logarithms
pj,tp_{j,t}pj,t​“p sub j comma t”the probability the model gave to token ttt of option jjj
ln⁡pj,t\ln p_{j,t}lnpj,t​“ell en of p sub j comma t”the log-probability of that one token. Always negative, because probabilities are below 1

4. Out loud. “The normalised score of an option is one over its number of tokens, times the sum of the log-probabilities of all its tokens.”

5. Worked. These seven numbers are made up for practice; no model produced them.

Two options. The short one is two tokens with log-probabilities -1.2 and -0.9. The long one is five tokens with log-probabilities -1.2, -0.9, -1.1, -0.8 and -1.0. That is two numbers plus five numbers, seven invented values in all.

Step 1, add up the short option’s log-probabilities.

−1.2+(−0.9)=−2.1-1.2 + (-0.9) = -2.1−1.2+(−0.9)=−2.1

Step 2, add up the long option’s.

−1.2+(−0.9)+(−1.1)+(−0.8)+(−1.0)=−5.0-1.2 + (-0.9) + (-1.1) + (-0.8) + (-1.0) = -5.0−1.2+(−0.9)+(−1.1)+(−0.8)+(−1.0)=−5.0

Step 3, compare the totals. -2.1 against -5.0. Since -2.1 is closer to zero, it is the larger number, so on totals the short option wins by a distance.

Step 4, divide each by its number of tokens.

ℓˉshort=−2.12=−2.1÷2=−1.05\bar{\ell}_{\text{short}} = \frac{-2.1}{2} = -2.1 \div 2 = -1.05ℓˉshort​=2−2.1​=−2.1÷2=−1.05
ℓˉlong=−5.05=−5.0÷5=−1.00\bar{\ell}_{\text{long}} = \frac{-5.0}{5} = -5.0 \div 5 = -1.00ℓˉlong​=5−5.0​=−5.0÷5=−1.00

Step 5, compare again. -1.00 is closer to zero than -1.05, so the long option now wins.

The ranking flipped. Nothing about the model’s opinion changed between step 3 and step 5. The only thing that changed was whether you compared totals or averages.

6. Check it. Every log-probability must be negative or zero, because every probability is between 0 and 1 and the logarithm of a number below 1 is negative. If one of yours is positive, you took the log of something that was not a probability.

The average must land between the smallest and the largest of the values you averaged. Here the long option’s values run from -1.2 to -0.8, and -1.00 sits inside that range. ✅ If your average falls outside the range of the numbers that made it, you divided by the wrong count.

Definition 13.5: Length normalisation

Length normalisation is dividing a total that was built up from several pieces by the number of pieces, so that things made of different numbers of pieces can be compared fairly. Here it turns a total log-probability into a per-token average, so a long answer is not penalised for being long.

Python¶

The loops below add up two short lists by hand, one number at a time, so you can see what the ∑\sum∑ in Formula 13.5 does. Then the last two lines print the real measured result.

# A made-up example, invented for practice, to show what dividing by the length does.
# These log-probabilities are not measurements. Nothing above this line produced them.
short_option_log_probabilities = [-1.2, -0.9]
long_option_log_probabilities = [-1.2, -0.9, -1.1, -0.8, -1.0]

# Add up the short option's log-probabilities with an explicit loop.
short_option_total = 0.0
for one_value in short_option_log_probabilities:
    short_option_total = short_option_total + one_value

# Add up the long option's log-probabilities the same way.
long_option_total = 0.0
for one_value in long_option_log_probabilities:
    long_option_total = long_option_total + one_value

print("short option, total    :", round(short_option_total, 4), "over", len(short_option_log_probabilities), "tokens")
print("long option, total     :", round(long_option_total, 4), "over", len(long_option_log_probabilities), "tokens")
print("short option, per token:", round(short_option_total / len(short_option_log_probabilities), 4))
print("long option, per token :", round(long_option_total / len(long_option_log_probabilities), 4))

# Now the real measurement, from the file.
option_text_counts = three_procedures["option_text_counts"]
print("real run, option-text procedure:", round(option_text_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent")
print("real run, which positions it chose:", option_text_counts)

Output:

short option, total    : -2.1 over 2 tokens
long option, total     : -5.0 over 5 tokens
short option, per token: -1.05
long option, per token : -1.0
real run, option-text procedure: 35.0 percent
real run, which positions it chose: {'A': 7, 'B': 11, 'C': 2, 'D': 0}

short_option_total = 0.0 sets up an empty running total before the loop starts. Then short_option_total = short_option_total + one_value adds the next number to it. Read that line right to left: take what the total currently holds, add the new value, store the answer back under the same name. A loop that does this is an accumulator, and it is how every ∑\sum∑ in this book is carried out in code. len(...) counts how many items are in a list.

Now the measured result, and it comes in two halves.

The good half. The score went from 25.0% to 35.0%. Seven questions out of twenty instead of five. That is two more questions, and it is ten percentage points above the chance level.

The half nobody prints. Look at where this procedure’s answers landed: A seven times, B eleven times, C twice, D never. Against an answer key of A two, B eight, C eight, D two.

It is a different bias. It is not a smaller one.

This procedure now over-chooses B, by a ratio of 11÷5=2.211 \div 5 = 2.211÷5=2.2. It still barely touches C, choosing it twice where the key rewards it eight times. It never once selects D. An unbiased procedure would land on each option about five times; this one produced 7, 11, 2 and 0.

So the honest report on fix one is: the score improved, and the instrument is still bent. It is bent in a new direction, which makes it harder to notice, because 35% does not sit suspiciously on the chance line the way 25% did.

That is the most dangerous kind of broken instrument: the one whose reading looks plausible.

13.5 Fix two: move the options around¶

Intuition¶

The second fix goes at the problem from the other end, and it is the more powerful of the two.

If you suspect the model is answering based on where an option sits, then move the options and see whether its answer follows. That is all. It is exactly what a careful teacher does when they suspect a student copied: they hand out the same test with the questions in a different order.

Here is the procedure in full. Take one question. Ask it four times. On the first asking, leave the options where they are. On the second, move every option up one place and wrap the top one round to the bottom, so what was option B is now option A. On the third, move them again. On the fourth, again. After four moves every option has occupied every position exactly once. That sliding-and-wrapping move is called a cyclic rotation.

Each time, you write down whether the model landed on the correct option, wherever the correct option happens to be sitting now. Then you take the majority: if the model was right on at least three of the four askings, the question counts as correct.

A model that knows an answer will follow that answer around the page. If it knows the mean of 2, 4, 4 and 6 is 4, it should select 4 whether 4 is sitting in slot A, B, C or D. A model that is reaching for a position will be right exactly once in four, because the correct option passes through its favourite slot exactly once during the rotation.

Read that last sentence again, because it is the sharp edge of this section. A model that always answers A scores one out of four on every single question under rotation, and one out of four is below the three-out-of-four majority, so it fails every question. Rotation does not soften position bias. It removes the reward for it entirely.

Applied to all twenty questions, the score came out at 15.0%. Three questions of twenty. Below the naive 25.0%. Below the option-text 35.0%.

Here is where you have to be careful, and it is the chapter’s own lesson turned back on the chapter. It is tempting to write “and 15.0% is below the chance level of 25%.” That sentence is wrong. The 25% chance level belongs to a procedure that asks each question once. This procedure asks each question four times and demands at least three hits, which is a much harder target for a guesser. A guesser facing this rule averages about 5.1%, not 25%, and Worked example 13.2 does that arithmetic in full. So 15.0% is in fact above chance for the procedure that produced it.

Changing the rule changed the chance level too. A chance level is a property of a procedure, in exactly the way a score is, and comparing a score from one procedure against a chance level computed for another is the same mistake in a smaller costume.

And the second number this procedure produces is the one that ends the argument. Of the twenty questions, the four rotations agreed with each other on exactly one.

The mathematics¶

Two formulas and one worked example. The first formula says where the correct answer moves to. The second is the punchline. The worked example settles what a guesser would score under this rule, which is the line the 15.0% has to be read against.

Formula 13.6: Where the correct answer sits after a rotation

1. In words. When you slide all the options up by some number of places and wrap the ones that fall off the top around to the bottom, the correct answer moves up by the same number of places, and it wraps around too. To find where it landed, subtract the number of places you slid, and if the answer goes below zero, add the number of options back on.

2. The formula.

gr=(g−r) mod kg_r = (g - r) \bmod kgr​=(g−r)modk

3. The symbols.

SymbolHow to say it out loudWhat it means
grg_rgr​“g sub r”the answer: which position the correct option occupies after rotation rrr
ggg“gee”which position the correct option started in. Counting from 0, so position 0 is option A, position 1 is option B, position 2 is C, position 3 is D. This is not the ggg of Formula 13.1, which stood for a scoring procedure. A letter gets re-used for a new job now and then, and when this book does that it says so
rrr“arr”how many places you slid the options. r=0r = 0r=0 means no slide
===“equals”the two sides are the same number
−-−“minus”subtract
the round brackets, (  )(\;)()“bracket, close bracket”do what is inside them first. So (g−r) mod k(g - r) \bmod k(g−r)modk means subtract first, then take the remainder
 mod \bmodmod“mod”, short for “modulo”the remainder after dividing. It is what makes the wrapping happen
kkk“kay”how many options there are, 4

A note on “mod”, which is one of the two unfamiliar symbols in this chapter. The other is the “choose” sign in Formula 13.11, and it gets the same treatment when it arrives.  mod \bmodmod means “take the remainder after dividing”. So 7 mod 4=37 \bmod 4 = 37mod4=3, because 7 divided by 4 is 1 with 3 left over. It is the arithmetic of a clock face: five hours after ten o’clock is three o’clock, because 15 mod 12=315 \bmod 12 = 315mod12=3. When the number underneath is negative, keep adding kkk until it is not: −1 mod 4=3-1 \bmod 4 = 3−1mod4=3, because −1+4=3-1 + 4 = 3−1+4=3.

4. Out loud. “The correct position after a rotation is the starting position minus the rotation number, with the remainder taken after dividing by the number of options.”

5. Worked, on question 1 of the bank. The question is “The mean of 2, 4, 4, 6 is:” and the options are 3, 4, 5, 6. The correct answer is 4, sitting in position 1, which is option B.

Rotation r=0r = 0r=0. No slide.

g0=(1−0) mod 4=1 mod 4=1→option Bg_0 = (1 - 0) \bmod 4 = 1 \bmod 4 = 1 \rightarrow \text{option B}g0​=(1−0)mod4=1mod4=1→option B

Rotation r=1r = 1r=1. The options become 4, 5, 6, 3.

g1=(1−1) mod 4=0 mod 4=0→option Ag_1 = (1 - 1) \bmod 4 = 0 \bmod 4 = 0 \rightarrow \text{option A}g1​=(1−1)mod4=0mod4=0→option A

Rotation r=2r = 2r=2. The options become 5, 6, 3, 4.

g2=(1−2) mod 4=(−1) mod 4=3→option Dg_2 = (1 - 2) \bmod 4 = (-1) \bmod 4 = 3 \rightarrow \text{option D}g2​=(1−2)mod4=(−1)mod4=3→option D

That third line is where the wrapping shows. 1−2=−11 - 2 = -11−2=−1, and −1+4=3-1 + 4 = 3−1+4=3, so the correct answer is now option D.

Rotation r=3r = 3r=3. The options become 6, 3, 4, 5.

g3=(1−3) mod 4=(−2) mod 4=2→option Cg_3 = (1 - 3) \bmod 4 = (-2) \bmod 4 = 2 \rightarrow \text{option C}g3​=(1−3)mod4=(−2)mod4=2→option C

6. Check it. Across the four rotations the correct answer must visit all four positions exactly once. Here it visited B, A, D, C. ✅ Every letter appears once. If one letter appears twice, you have a mistake in the mod arithmetic, and the usual cause is not adding kkk back on when the subtraction went negative.

Formula 13.7: The consistency rate under rotation

1. In words. Count how many questions the four rotations agreed on, meaning the model was right all four times or wrong all four times. Divide by the number of questions. That gives you the share of questions where the model behaved the same way no matter where the options sat.

2. The formula.

c^=un\hat{c} = \frac{u}{n}c^=nu​

3. The symbols.

SymbolHow to say it out loudWhat it means
c^\hat{c}c^“c hat”the answer: the consistency rate, between 0 and 1. This is not the ccc of Formula 13.2, which was the chance level. The hat is the clue: this one was measured
the hat“hat”a mark meaning “measured, not known for certain”
===“equals”the two sides are the same number
uuu“you”how many questions the four rotations agreed on: right four times, or wrong four times
the fraction bar“divided by”divide the top by the bottom
nnn“en”the number of questions, 20

4. Out loud. “The consistency rate is the number of questions the rotations agreed on, divided by the number of questions.”

5. Worked, on the real run. The lab measured u=1u = 1u=1 out of n=20n = 20n=20.

c^=120=1÷20=0.05,0.05×100=5.0%\hat{c} = \frac{1}{20} = 1 \div 20 = 0.05, \qquad 0.05 \times 100 = 5.0\%c^=201​=1÷20=0.05,0.05×100=5.0%

Now work out what a position-locked model would score, so you have something to compare against. Suppose a model always picks position A, whatever the question says. On each question the correct answer passes through position A exactly once in the four rotations, so the model is right once and wrong three times. That is neither four-out-of-four nor zero-out-of-four, so the rotations disagree, and the question is not consistent.

c^always-A=020=0.0\hat{c}_{\text{always-A}} = \frac{0}{20} = 0.0c^always-A​=200​=0.0

And a model that genuinely knows the material is right on all four rotations of every question it knows, so those questions are consistent.

So the consistency rate runs from 0, for a model that is purely following positions, up towards 1, for a model that is actually reading the options. The measured 0.05 sits almost at the bottom of that range.

6. Check it. uuu cannot exceed nnn, so c^\hat{c}c^ cannot exceed 1. And here is a check on your understanding rather than your arithmetic: a low consistency rate is not the same as a low score. A model could be consistently wrong on every question, always picking the same incorrect option, and score 0% with a consistency rate of 1.0. That would tell you it had a firm, wrong opinion. A consistency rate near zero tells you something different and worse: the answers are not opinions at all.

Worked example 13.2: The chance level of the rotation procedure

Formula 13.2 said the chance level with four options is 1÷4=0.251 \div 4 = 0.251÷4=0.25. That was for a procedure that asks each question once. The rotation procedure asks four times and requires at least three hits. Work out what a guesser averages under that rule.

Step 1, the chance of one asking. Four options, one right, so 1÷4=0.251 \div 4 = 0.251÷4=0.25, and the chance of missing is 1−0.25=0.751 - 0.25 = 0.751−0.25=0.75.

Step 2, list the outcomes that count as correct. The rule needs 3 or 4 hits out of 4. So there are two outcomes to add up: exactly 3 hits, and exactly 4 hits.

Step 3, exactly 4 hits. All four askings have to land. Multiply 0.25 by itself four times.

0.25×0.25=0.06250.25 \times 0.25 = 0.06250.25×0.25=0.0625
0.0625×0.25=0.0156250.0625 \times 0.25 = 0.0156250.0625×0.25=0.015625
0.015625×0.25=0.003906250.015625 \times 0.25 = 0.003906250.015625×0.25=0.00390625

Step 4, exactly 3 hits. Three askings land and one misses, which is 0.25×0.25×0.25×0.750.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.750.25×0.25×0.25×0.75.

0.25×0.25×0.25=0.0156250.25 \times 0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.0156250.25×0.25×0.25=0.015625
0.015625×0.75=0.011718750.015625 \times 0.75 = 0.011718750.015625×0.75=0.01171875

But the miss could be any one of the four askings, so there are four ways this can happen. That count is the “choose” sign of Formula 13.11 doing a small job: (43)=4\binom{4}{3} = 4(34​)=4.

4×0.01171875=0.0468754 \times 0.01171875 = 0.0468754×0.01171875=0.046875

Step 5, add the two outcomes.

0.046875+0.00390625=0.050781250.046875 + 0.00390625 = 0.050781250.046875+0.00390625=0.05078125

Step 6, as a percentage.

0.05078125×100=5.078125%, which rounds to 5.1%0.05078125 \times 100 = 5.078125\%, \text{ which rounds to } 5.1\%0.05078125×100=5.078125%, which rounds to 5.1%

The check. The answer has to be smaller than the single-asking chance level of 25%, because the rule asks for three hits where before it asked for one, and asking for more cannot make guessing easier. And 5.1% is smaller than 25%. ✅ A second check: written as a fraction the answer is 13÷25613 \div 25613÷256, and 256=28256 = 2^8256=28, which is a whole number of halvings, so the arithmetic is exact rather than rounded.

One assumption, stated. Steps 3 and 4 multiply the four askings together, and multiplying probabilities like that assumes the four askings do not influence each other. For a guesser that is true. For a real model it is not: a model with a habit will lean the same way every time. So 5.1% is the chance level for guessing, which is what a chance level is for, and it is not a prediction about any particular model.

What it means. The measured 15.0% is about three times the 5.1% a guesser would average under this rule. Read against its own chance level, the rotation score is not a chance result. It is a low score, from a weak model, on a procedure that no longer pays for a position habit. The rotation procedure is also the one the two-model comparison in section 13.7 runs on, so knowing where its chance line sits is worth the two minutes.

Read the definition of a metric before you quote it

The consistency count in lab/out/we6b_eval_debiased.json counts a question as consistent when the four rotations agreed on the verdict: right all four times, or wrong all four times. You can read that in the script, lab/we6b_eval_debiased.py, in the line if sum(votes) in (0, 4).

That is subtly different from “gave the same answer all four times”. A model could be wrong four times while giving four different wrong answers, and this measure would count it as consistent.

The distinction does not change the conclusion here, because of the argument worked in Formula 13.7: a model locked onto one position is right exactly once in four and therefore counts as inconsistent under this measure. So a consistency of 1 out of 20 is, if anything, harsher on the model than the looser phrase would be.

This point belongs in a chapter about measuring your measurement, and it applies to this book as much as to anyone else’s. A metric is a procedure. Read its definition before you quote its number, including when the number is ours.

Definition 13.6: Cyclic rotation

A cyclic rotation slides every option along by a fixed number of places and wraps the ones that fall off the end back round to the start. After kkk rotations of a kkk-option question, every option has occupied every position exactly once.

Definition 13.7: Majority vote

A majority vote asks the same question several times under different conditions and keeps the answer that won more than half the askings. Here, a question counts as correct when the model landed on the right option in at least 3 of the 4 rotations.

Python¶

# Question 1 of the bank, with its four options in their printed order.
option_list = ["3", "4", "5", "6"]
letter_list = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]

# The right answer is 4, which sits in position 1, because Python counts from 0.
correct_position = 1

for rotation_number in range(option_count):
    # Rotate left: take everything from rotation_number onward, then everything before it.
    rotated_options = option_list[rotation_number:] + option_list[:rotation_number]
    # Work out where the right answer has moved to. The % sign is remainder after division.
    new_correct_position = (correct_position - rotation_number) % option_count
    print("rotation", rotation_number, rotated_options,
          " the right answer is now option", letter_list[new_correct_position])

# The two measured results of doing this to all 20 questions.
consistent_questions = three_procedures["fully_consistent_questions"]
print("score under majority-of-four-rotations:", round(rotation_accuracy * 100, 1), "percent")
print("questions where all four rotations agreed:", consistent_questions, "of", question_count)
print("that is", round(100 * consistent_questions / question_count, 1), "percent consistent")

Output:

rotation 0 ['3', '4', '5', '6']  the right answer is now option B
rotation 1 ['4', '5', '6', '3']  the right answer is now option A
rotation 2 ['5', '6', '3', '4']  the right answer is now option D
rotation 3 ['6', '3', '4', '5']  the right answer is now option C
score under majority-of-four-rotations: 15.0 percent
questions where all four rotations agreed: 1 of 20
that is 5.0 percent consistent

Three pieces of Python are new here.

option_list[rotation_number:] takes a slice of a list: everything from that position to the end. option_list[:rotation_number] takes everything before that position. Gluing the two together with + performs the rotation. On the second pass, rotation_number is 1, so the first slice is ['4','5','6'], the second is ['3'], and together they make ['4','5','6','3'].

% between two whole numbers is the remainder after division, which is the  mod \bmodmod from Formula 13.6. In Python, (1 - 2) % 4 gives 3, with the wrapping already handled for you.

range(option_count) produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3. It stops before the number you give it, which catches everybody once.

Now the output. The first four lines show the correct answer visiting B, A, D and C, one position per rotation, exactly as Formula 13.6 predicted.

The last three lines are the real result, and the middle one is the most important number in this chapter.

One question out of twenty.

On nineteen of the twenty questions, moving the options around changed whether the model was right. Its answers were not opinions about statistics that happened to be wrong. They were responses to the layout of the page.

At this point you have three numbers, 25.0%, 35.0% and 15.0%, and you could defend any one of them in writing. But the consistency count tells you what the honest report is, and it is not a number at all. It is a sentence: this model does not know this material, and a single figure should not have been printed.

That sentence is worth more than any of the three percentages. It is also the sentence that never appears on a leaderboard.

The simulation¶

Everything in sections 13.1 through 13.5 is in the page below, and you can move between the two views with the slider. View 0 puts the three procedures side by side against the chance level. View 1 is the diagnosis: for each letter, how often the model chose it against how often it was the right answer.

Try it 13.1: Predict before you look

Before you move the slider, answer these three on paper.

  1. A model that had genuinely learned this material would produce a letter-count spread close to which four numbers?

  2. If a scoring procedure chose option C zero times out of twenty, what is the highest score it could possibly reach on this bank?

  3. The naive procedure scored 25.0% and the rotation procedure scored 15.0%. Which of the two is closer to the truth about what this model knows, and why is that a trick question?

Solution

1. Close to the answer key: A two, B eight, C eight, D two. A model reading the options should land on the right answer often, and the right answers are spread that way. A spread close to five each would suggest a model guessing without a position preference, which is different from a model that knows the material.

2. The correct answer is C on eight of the twenty questions, and a procedure that never chooses C gets every one of those wrong. That leaves twelve questions it could possibly get right, so the ceiling is 12÷20=0.6012 \div 20 = 0.6012÷20=0.60, which is 60%. The naive procedure has a built-in maximum of 60% on this bank, and nothing the model knows can raise it. Worth sitting with: a reported score has a ceiling set by the procedure, and the ceiling is almost never mentioned.

3. It is a trick question because “closer to the truth” assumes there is a single true number to be close to, and the consistency count of 1 out of 20 says there is not. The rotation procedure is the better procedure, because it cannot be fooled by a position preference. But its output of 15.0% is not a truer estimate of the model’s knowledge; it is a more honest statement that there is nothing here to estimate. The right answer to “what does this model score” is “under what procedure, and with what interval, and here is the consistency count.”

13.6 Position bias is a symptom of weakness, not a fixed tax¶

Intuition¶

A reasonable reader reaches this point and draws the wrong conclusion. It goes like this: “Position bias inflates naive scores. So every naive score is inflated by roughly ten points, and I should mentally subtract ten from anything I read.”

That would be tidy. It is also wrong, and the evidence against it is in the course lab.

The same twenty questions were put to three models from the same family: the 0.5B, the 1.5B and the 3B. Same questions, same prompts, same code, same machine. Size is the only thing that changes, which makes this a controlled experiment in the ordinary scientific sense. Each model was scored twice, once by the naive letter procedure and once by the rotation procedure. The distance between those two scores is what this section calls the debiasing gap.

Here is what the gap did as the models got bigger.

At 0.5B, the gap is 10 points: 25.0% naive, 15.0% rotated. At 1.5B, the gap is 10 points: 80.0% naive, 70.0% rotated. At 3B, the gap is 0 points: 95.0% naive, 95.0% rotated.

The largest model’s score does not move when you take the position bias away. Rotating the options changes nothing, because it was never answering on position in the first place.

And look at how the 3B distributed its first-pick answers: B eight times, C seven, D twice, A three times. Now put the answer key beside it: B eight, C eight, D two, A two. Those two lines are nearly the same line. The model is not picking positions. It is picking answers, and the answers happen to sit where they sit.

The consistency counts tell the same story from the other side. Under four rotations, the number of questions where all four rotations agreed on the verdict went 1, then 13, then 18, out of twenty.

So position bias is not a tax levied on all benchmark scores. It is a symptom that appears when a model does not know the answer. When a model has no view about which option is right, the only thing left to break the tie is a habit, and a preference for the letter A is such a habit. When the model does have a view, the habit is overridden and the bias vanishes on its own.

That reframes the diagnosis in section 13.3. The 16-out-of-20 A count was not a separate defect sitting alongside a weak model. It was what a weak model looks like when you score it that way.

The mathematics¶

Formula 13.8: The debiasing gap

1. In words. Score the model twice, once with the naive procedure and once with a procedure that removes the position preference. Subtract the second score from the first. A large answer means the naive score was propped up by something other than knowledge. An answer of zero means the position preference was not doing any work.

2. The formula.

Δ=p^(naive)−p^(rot)\Delta = \hat{p}^{(\text{naive})} - \hat{p}^{(\text{rot})}Δ=p^​(naive)−p^​(rot)

3. The symbols.

SymbolHow to say it out loudWhat it means
Δ\DeltaΔ“delta”a capital Greek D. In this book it marks a difference between two things. Here, the answer. See the toolkit on Greek letters
===“equals”the two sides are the same number
p^(naive)\hat{p}^{(\text{naive})}p^​(naive)“p hat under naive”the accuracy under the naive letter procedure
p^(rot)\hat{p}^{(\text{rot})}p^​(rot)“p hat under rot”the accuracy under the rotation procedure
the raised label in brackets“under”a label naming a procedure, never a power
−-−“minus”subtract the second from the first

4. Out loud. “The debiasing gap is the naive accuracy minus the rotation accuracy.”

5. Worked, on all three models.

The 0.5B model.

Δ=0.25−0.15=0.10,0.10×100=10.0 percentage points\Delta = 0.25 - 0.15 = 0.10, \qquad 0.10 \times 100 = 10.0 \text{ percentage points}Δ=0.25−0.15=0.10,0.10×100=10.0 percentage points

The 1.5B model.

Δ=0.80−0.70=0.10,0.10×100=10.0 percentage points\Delta = 0.80 - 0.70 = 0.10, \qquad 0.10 \times 100 = 10.0 \text{ percentage points}Δ=0.80−0.70=0.10,0.10×100=10.0 percentage points

The 3B model.

Δ=0.95−0.95=0.00,0.00×100=0.0 percentage points\Delta = 0.95 - 0.95 = 0.00, \qquad 0.00 \times 100 = 0.0 \text{ percentage points}Δ=0.95−0.95=0.00,0.00×100=0.0 percentage points

6. Check it. Δ\DeltaΔ can be negative, and that is informative rather than an error: it would mean the debiased procedure scored higher, which happens when a model’s position habit was pushing it away from correct answers rather than towards them.

The honest caution, and it belongs here rather than in a footnote. Each of these numbers comes from twenty questions. A difference of one question is 5 percentage points on a bank this size. The file lab/out/lab4_size_ladder.json carries a measured standard error for each rotation score, and they are large: 0.0798 at 0.5B, 0.1025 at 1.5B and 0.0487 at 3B, which as percentage points is 8.0, 10.2 and 4.9. Every score in this section should be read with a wobble of about that size around it. The 0-point gap at 3B is built on the model getting 19 of 20 both times. If the 3B had missed one extra question under rotation, the gap would read 5 points instead of 0. So the shape of the ladder, large gap at the bottom and no gap at the top, is the finding here. The precise gap values are far less certain than printing them to one decimal place suggests, and Chapter 12 is the chapter that taught you why.

Definition 13.8: Debiasing gap

The debiasing gap is the naive score minus the debiased score, in percentage points. A large gap says the naive procedure was rewarding a position habit. A gap of zero says the model was answering the question.

Python¶

print("model                          naive   rotation    gap   consistent   first-pick spread")
for model_name in size_ladder:
    one_model = size_ladder[model_name]
    naive_for_this_model = one_model["naive_accuracy"]
    rotation_for_this_model = one_model["rotation_accuracy"]
    # The debiasing gap: how much the naive number fell when the bias was taken away.
    gap_in_points = round((naive_for_this_model - rotation_for_this_model) * 100, 1)
    short_name = model_name.split("/")[1]
    print(short_name.ljust(30),
          str(round(naive_for_this_model * 100, 1)).rjust(5),
          str(round(rotation_for_this_model * 100, 1)).rjust(9),
          str(gap_in_points).rjust(7),
          (str(one_model["consistent"]) + " of 20").rjust(12),
          "  ", one_model["first_pick_spread"])

print("the answer key spread, for comparison:", answer_key_counts)

Output:

model                          naive   rotation    gap   consistent   first-pick spread
Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct           25.0      15.0    10.0      1 of 20    {'A': 16, 'D': 2, 'B': 2}
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct           80.0      70.0    10.0     13 of 20    {'C': 7, 'B': 7, 'D': 2, 'A': 4}
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct             95.0      95.0     0.0     18 of 20    {'B': 8, 'C': 7, 'D': 2, 'A': 3}
the answer key spread, for comparison: {'A': 2, 'B': 8, 'C': 8, 'D': 2}

for model_name in size_ladder walks through the labels in the loaded dictionary, one per model. model_name.split("/")[1] cuts the text Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at the slash and keeps the second piece, so the table is readable. .ljust(30) and .rjust(5) pad text on the right or the left so the columns line up.

Read this table from the bottom up.

The last row and the last line. {'B': 8, 'C': 7, 'D': 2, 'A': 3} against the key’s {'A': 2, 'B': 8, 'C': 8, 'D': 2}. B matches exactly at 8. C is off by one, 7 against 8. D matches exactly at 2. A is off by one, 3 against 2. A model that is reading the options produces an answer spread that looks like the answer key, and this one does.

The first row. {'A': 16, 'D': 2, 'B': 2}, with C missing entirely because it was never chosen. A model that is not reading the options produces a spread that looks like a habit.

The consistent column. 1, then 13, then 18, out of twenty. These are the questions where all four rotations agreed on the verdict, in the precise sense set out in section 13.5. This is the cleanest single column in the table. It rises with size and it rises fast, and it is the column that tells you whether the answers mean anything before you look at any score.

The gap column. 10.0, 10.0, 0.0. The gap does not fall smoothly. It holds at ten points across a threefold increase in size and then goes to zero. Twenty questions is nowhere near enough data to say anything about the shape of that fall, and this book will not pretend otherwise. What the column does support is the qualitative claim: the gap is present when the model is weak and absent when it is strong.

Try it 13.2: Reading the ladder

Using only the printed table:

  1. The 1.5B model chose A four times out of twenty. Compute its over-choice ratio for A, using Formula 13.4.

  2. The 0.5B chose A sixteen times. Compute the same ratio, and say how many times larger it is.

  3. Somebody claims “the 1.5B still has a position bias, because its naive and rotation scores differ by 10 points.” Is the letter spread consistent with that claim?

Solution

1. The expected count is E=n/k=20÷4=5E = n/k = 20 \div 4 = 5E=n/k=20÷4=5. So

RA=45=4÷5=0.8R_A = \frac{4}{5} = 4 \div 5 = 0.8RA​=54​=4÷5=0.8

That is below 1, meaning the 1.5B chose A slightly less often than an unbiased procedure would.

2. For the 0.5B,

RA=165=16÷5=3.2R_A = \frac{16}{5} = 16 \div 5 = 3.2RA​=516​=16÷5=3.2

And 3.2÷0.8=4.03.2 \div 0.8 = 4.03.2÷0.8=4.0, so the smaller model’s over-choice of A is four times the larger model’s.

3. The letter spread does not support a simple A-preference for the 1.5B. Its spread is {'C': 7, 'B': 7, 'D': 2, 'A': 4}, which is close to the key on D and not wildly off on the others, and it under-chooses A rather than over-choosing it. So whatever is costing the 1.5B those 10 points under rotation is not a plain preference for the first option. It is more likely that on the questions it does not know, its answer is unstable, and instability costs you under a majority-of-four rule. You could check that directly by pulling out the per-question rotation votes, which is Stretch problem 21 at the end of this chapter.

13.7 Comparing two models: the wrong way, then the right way¶

Intuition¶

Everything so far has been about one model. Almost every real question is about two.

Should the department install the 1.5B or the 3B? The 3B is more accurate and costs more energy per token, a trade-off Chapter 7 measured. But before that trade-off is even worth discussing, somebody has to establish that the 3B is actually better, and by how much, and with what certainty.

The two models sat the same twenty questions, under the same rotation-debiased procedure.

  • Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct scored 14 of 20, which is 70.0%.

  • Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct scored 19 of 20, which is 95.0%.

  • The gap is 25.0 percentage points.

Now, how uncertain is that 25-point gap? There are two ways to work it out and they differ in one assumption.

The unpaired way treats the two results as two separate surveys. You worked out the wobble for one model’s score in Chapter 12; do that twice and combine. This is the standard formula for comparing two proportions and it is in every introductory statistics book.

It is also the wrong tool here, and the reason is a single sentence: the two models answered the same questions.

Think about what that means. Question 5 of the bank is hard, or it is easy, and it is exactly as hard or as easy for both models. That shared difficulty is not noise to be averaged away. It is information you paid for by using the same bank, and the unpaired formula throws it in the bin.

The paired way keeps it. Go through the questions one at a time and write down, for each one, what the 3B did minus what the 1.5B did. That difference can only be three things: +1 if the 3B got it right and the 1.5B did not, -1 if the reverse, and 0 if they did the same thing.

Then average those twenty differences. The average comes out to exactly the same 25 points, as it always must. But the spread of the differences is smaller than the spread of the two separate scores, because every question the models agreed on contributes a 0, and zeros pull a spread down.

Smaller spread, smaller standard error, narrower interval. Same data, better answer, no extra questions asked.

The mathematics¶

Two formulas here. The first is the unpaired standard error, shown so you can see what it costs. The second is the paired one.

Formula 13.9: The unpaired standard error of a difference

1. In words. Work out the wobble in each model’s score separately. Add the two wobbles together, inside the square root, and take the square root of the total. This is how you would do it if the two models had sat two different tests.

2. The formula.

SEunpaired=p^A(1−p^A)n+p^B(1−p^B)nSE_{\text{unpaired}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_A(1 - \hat{p}_A)}{n} + \frac{\hat{p}_B(1 - \hat{p}_B)}{n}}SEunpaired​=np^​A​(1−p^​A​)​+np^​B​(1−p^​B​)​​

3. The symbols.

SymbolHow to say it out loudWhat it means
SEunpairedSE_{\text{unpaired}}SEunpaired​“ess ee unpaired”the answer: how much the measured gap would wobble on a re-run, computed the wrong way for this data
===“equals”the two sides are the same number
x\sqrt{\phantom{x}}x​“the square root of”the number which, multiplied by itself, gives what is underneath. 9=3\sqrt{9} = 39​=3 because 3×3=93 \times 3 = 93×3=9. It covers the whole sum here, not one piece. See the toolkit on square roots
p^A\hat{p}_Ap^​A​“p hat sub A”model A’s accuracy. Here the 1.5B, at 0.70. From this formula onwards, AAA and BBB name the two models. They are no longer the options A and B on a question
p^B\hat{p}_Bp^​B​“p hat sub B”model B’s accuracy. Here the 3B, at 0.95
1−p^A1 - \hat{p}_A1−p^​A​“one minus p hat sub A”the share model A got wrong. Here 1−0.70=0.301 - 0.70 = 0.301−0.70=0.30
1−p^B1 - \hat{p}_B1−p^​B​“one minus p hat sub B”the share model B got wrong. Here 1−0.95=0.051 - 0.95 = 0.051−0.95=0.05
×\times×, written as juxtaposition“times”p^A(1−p^A)\hat{p}_A(1 - \hat{p}_A)p^​A​(1−p^​A​) means multiply those two together. See the toolkit on multiplication
the fraction bars“divided by”divide each top by its own bottom
nnn“en”the number of questions, 20 for both
+++“plus”add the two pieces together, inside the square root

4. Out loud. “The unpaired standard error is the square root of: model A’s accuracy times one minus it, divided by the number of questions, plus model B’s accuracy times one minus it, divided by the number of questions.”

5. Worked, step by step.

Step 1, model A’s piece, with p^A=0.70\hat{p}_A = 0.70p^​A​=0.70.

1−0.70=0.301 - 0.70 = 0.301−0.70=0.30

0.70×0.30=0.210.70 \times 0.30 = 0.210.70×0.30=0.21

0.21÷20=0.0105000.21 \div 20 = 0.0105000.21÷20=0.010500

Step 2, model B’s piece, with p^B=0.95\hat{p}_B = 0.95p^​B​=0.95.

1−0.95=0.051 - 0.95 = 0.051−0.95=0.05

0.95×0.05=0.04750.95 \times 0.05 = 0.04750.95×0.05=0.0475

0.0475÷20=0.0023750.0475 \div 20 = 0.0023750.0475÷20=0.002375

Step 3, add the two pieces.

0.010500+0.002375=0.0128750.010500 + 0.002375 = 0.0128750.010500+0.002375=0.012875

Step 4, take the square root.

0.012875=0.113468\sqrt{0.012875} = 0.1134680.012875​=0.113468

Step 5, build the 95% interval around the measured gap of 0.25. The multiplier 1.96 is the one Chapter 12 introduced for 95%.

1.96×0.113468=0.2223971.96 \times 0.113468 = 0.2223971.96×0.113468=0.222397

0.25−0.222397=0.0276030.25 - 0.222397 = 0.0276030.25−0.222397=0.027603

0.25+0.222397=0.4723970.25 + 0.222397 = 0.4723970.25+0.222397=0.472397

Those two numbers are shares, between 0 and 1. Turn each into percentage points by multiplying by 100, the same move as in Worked example 13.1.

0.027603×100=2.76030.027603 \times 100 = 2.76030.027603×100=2.7603, which rounds to 2.8

0.472397×100=47.23970.472397 \times 100 = 47.23970.472397×100=47.2397, which rounds to 47.2

As percentage points, the interval is (+2.8,+47.2)(+2.8, +47.2)(+2.8,+47.2). Two numbers inside round brackets with a comma between them is how this book writes an interval: the first number is the bottom end, the second is the top end, and the claim is that the true gap sits somewhere between them. See the toolkit on inequalities and intervals.

6. Check it. The whole thing lives under one square root. A common slip is taking the root of each piece and then adding, which gives 0.0105+0.002375=0.1025+0.0487=0.1512\sqrt{0.0105} + \sqrt{0.002375} = 0.1025 + 0.0487 = 0.15120.0105​+0.002375​=0.1025+0.0487=0.1512, a different and wrong answer. If your standard error is bigger than about 0.15 on a twenty-question bank, check that first.

And read what the interval says: the gap is somewhere between about 3 points and about 47 points. It excludes zero, so on this analysis you would report a real difference. Hold that thought.

Formula 13.10: The paired difference, its spread, and its interval

1. In words. For each question, subtract what the first model scored from what the second model scored, giving you one number per question. Average those. Then measure how much they vary around that average, divide that by the square root of the number of questions, and build the interval the usual way.

2. The formulas. There are four, and they run one into the next.

di=ci(B)−ci(A)d_i = c_i^{(B)} - c_i^{(A)}di​=ci(B)​−ci(A)​
dˉ=1n∑i=1ndi\bar{d} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_idˉ=n1​i=1∑n​di​
sd=1n−1∑i=1n(di−dˉ)2,SEdˉ=sdns_d = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(d_i - \bar{d}\right)^2}, \qquad SE_{\bar{d}} = \frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}sd​=n−11​i=1∑n​(di​−dˉ)2​,SEdˉ​=n​sd​​
interval=dˉ±1.96×SEdˉ\text{interval} = \bar{d} \pm 1.96 \times SE_{\bar{d}}interval=dˉ±1.96×SEdˉ​

3. The symbols.

1n\dfrac{1}{n}n1​ and the sum written side by side“times”two things written next to each other with no sign between them means multiply them. See the toolkit on multiplication

the raised 2“squared”multiply the thing by itself. See the toolkit on exponents

n\sqrt{n}n​“the square root of en”20=4.472136\sqrt{20} = 4.47213620​=4.472136
